episodes.title: Before 1228: Mong Mao and the Tai political world
1540-1639: Koch, Mughals and the Asurar Ali frontier

events.title: Ahom origin tradition: Khunlung and Khunlai
events.summary: Ahom chronicles open with a divine-descent tradition in which the ancestors Khunlung and Khunlai come down from heaven to found Tai ruling lineages. This is a dynastic legitimation tradition, not datable history.

confidence.basis: Chronicle origin myth; present explicitly as tradition.

events.title: The Tai political world of the upper Shweli (Mong Mao)

date.calendarNote: Context window, not an event date.

events.summary: Tai-speaking principalities (mong) occupied valleys between the Irrawaddy and Yunnan. Mong Mao in the Shweli valley is the polity Ahom tradition links to Sukaphaa. Its 13th-century extent and institutions are poorly documented; its later expansion as Luchuan belongs to the 14th century and must not be projected backwards.

sourceRefs.locator: Ahoms as Shans from the ancient kingdom of Pong; Tai self-name

confidence.basis: Thin evidence for the 13th century; reliant on later chronicles and secondary synthesis.

disputes: Extent and capital of Mong Mao c.1200 are not established.
Risk of anachronism: Luchuan's 14th-century power under Si Kefa should not be shown for 1215.

events.title: Sukaphaa leaves the Tai homeland

date.calendarNote: Chronicle-derived date reproduced by Gait; converted from Tai reckoning.

events.summary: According to the Buranjis, as summarised by Gait, the prince Sukaphaa left Maulung in 1215 with nobles and followers, beginning years of wandering in the Patkai hills. Gait saw no reason to doubt the Buranji statement that he came from Maulung, within the old Shan kingdom he calls Pong. His reasons for leaving rest on tradition.

confidence.basis: Date is chronicle-derived; motive and homeland identification disputed.

numericClaims.value: eight nobles and 9,000 men, women and children
numericClaims.attribution: Buranji figure reported by Gait, who adds that most followers were probably adult men

disputes: Homeland: 'Maulung' / Mong Mit / Mong Mao identifications differ.
Motive (succession dispute) is traditional.

Gait (p. 73) notes that Shan chronicles do not mention Sukapha's invasion, but credit Samlungpha, brother of a Mungmau king who came to the throne in 1220, with victories in Upper Assam; Gait thinks both stories may be true.

events.title: Thirteen years in the Patkai hills
events.summary: The Buranjis, as summarised by Gait, say Sukaphaa spent thirteen years moving through the hilly Patkai country, raiding Naga villages, before reaching Khamjang in 1228. He crossed the Khamnamjang river on rafts and came to the Nongnyang lake. The chronicles name places, not a path, so any line drawn is a schematic corridor.

sourceRefs.locator: thirteen years in the Patkai; Khamjang; Khamnamjang river; Nongnyang lake

confidence.basis: Named waypoints from chronicles; route geometry reconstructed.

editorLog.note: Gait p. 74 verified (OCR): 13 years in the Patkai; arrival at Khamjang 1228; Naga raids. Route still unrecorded.

events.title: Arrival in the Brahmaputra valley (1228)

date.calendarNote: Conventional founding date of the Ahom kingdom; chronicle-derived.

events.summary: In 1228 Sukaphaa reached Khamjang, according to the Buranjis as summarised by Gait. From there his party moved on through Dangkaorang and Khamhangpung to Namrup, on the edge of the upper Brahmaputra valley. 1228 is the date conventionally used for the start of Ahom rule.

sourceRefs.locator: arrival in Khamjang 1228; Dangkaorang, Khamhangpung, Namrup

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

events.title: Search for a seat: Tipam, Abhaypur, Habung, Simaluguri
events.summary: Gait's summary of the Buranjis gives a dated sequence. Sukaphaa bridged the Sessa, tried the Dihing, then settled at Tipam. In 1236 he moved to Mungklang Chekhru (Abhaypur); a flood in 1240 drove him down the Brahmaputra to Habung, where his people lived by cultivation; another flood in 1244 pushed him on to the Dikhu mouth and Ligirigaon; in 1246 he moved to Simaluguri. Several of these places can only be located approximately.

sourceRefs.locator: Tipam; Mungklang Chekhru (Abhaypur) 1236; Habung 1240; Ligirigaon 1244; Simaluguri 1246

confidence.basis: Dated sequence verified in Gait p. 75 (chronicle-derived); locations partly approximate.

events.title: Violence against the Nagas of the Patkai

date.calendarNote: Placed by Gait at the Nongnyang lake stage, after arrival in Khamjang in 1228.

events.summary: Some Nagas resisted the newcomers. The Buranjis, as summarised by Gait, record that Sukaphaa defeated them and treated captives with extreme cruelty to terrify the surrounding villages into submission, and that he left a noble to rule the conquered area. Gait himself condemns these methods. The episode is part of the founding story and should be told plainly, without graphic visuals.

sourceRefs.locator: Naga resistance at Nongnyang; Gait's verdict on Sukapha

confidence.basis: Recorded in the Ahom chronicles and reported by Gait; one-sided source, but self-incriminating rather than flattering to the dynasty.

disputes: Details come only from the Ahom side; no Naga account survives in written form.

animationInstructions.text: The chronicles record violent conquest of Naga villages

editorLog.note: Added after Gait p. 74 verification; omitted in the Phase 1 draft.

events.title: Morans and Borahis incorporated
events.summary: The country around the new settlements belonged to the Morans, whose king Gait names as Badancha, and the Borahis, ruled by Thakumtha. Sukaphaa fought and defeated both, then, in Gait's account, adopted conciliatory policies, treating them as equals and encouraging intermarriage. Their numbers and the exact area involved are not recorded.

sourceRefs.locator: Morans under Badancha, Borahis under Thakumtha

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

territorialEffect.subject: moran
territorialEffect.notes: Area unknown; show as influence zone only.

events.title: Charaideo becomes the seat of the kingdom
events.summary: Charaideo became the first established seat of Ahom rule. It later became the royal burial ground, whose moidams are now a UNESCO World Heritage property.

confidence.basis: Gait p. 75 verified (chronicle-derived date); site confirmed by UNESCO inscription.

events.title: Death of Sukaphaa
events.summary: Sukaphaa died in 1268. Gait credits him with creating the two great offices of state, the Bar Gohain and the Burha Gohain, and notes that the Ahoms called the country Mungdunsunkham, 'the country full of golden gardens'.

sourceRefs.locator: death of Sukapha, 1268; Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain appointed

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

events.title: Wet-rice settlement and the growth of a valley state
events.summary: Over the following centuries the Ahom polity extended wet-rice cultivation and absorbed neighbouring groups, building the agrarian base of the later state. This is a long process, not a single event, and is shown as gradual settlement rather than a border.

sourceRefs.locator: at Habung 'the Ahoms lived by cultivation'
sourceRefs.note: Only a brief early reference; the long-run process needs Guha or Barpujari vol. 3.

sourceRefs.locator: essays on Ahom polity and economy

confidence.basis: Interpretive synthesis in standard scholarship.

events.title: Early Ahom-Chutia conflict
events.summary: Relations with the Chutia kingdom alternated between peace and war. Gait records frequent disputes under Sutuphaa, and says that in 1376 the Chutia king visited him at Chapaguri, pretending reconciliation, and killed him. An interregnum followed (1376-1380 in Gait's table).

confidence.basis: Gait pp. 78-79 verified (chronicle account).

events.title: Sudangphaa's reign
events.summary: Sudangphaa, remembered as Bamuni Konwar because tradition says he was raised in a Brahmin household, reigned around 1397-1407. His reign is associated with growing Brahmin influence at court.

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

disputes: Upbringing story is traditional.

events.title: Suhungmung (Dihingia Raja) becomes king
events.summary: Suhungmung, also known as Dihingia Raja, began a reign that saw a major territorial expansion of the kingdom.

sourceRefs.locator: Appendix: 'Chronology of Ahom Kings' (exact page within range not resolvable from OCR)

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

events.title: Annexation of the Chutia kingdom

alternatives.note: Some later works give 1524; Gait gives 1523.

events.summary: After fighting from 1518, the Chutias besieged an Ahom fort in 1523 and were routed. Gait's account says their king and his eldest son were killed, the royal family captured, and the whole Chutia country annexed under a new officer, the Sadiya Khowa Gohain. Ahom settlers were moved from Garhgaon to Sadiya to hold it.

sourceRefs.locator: Chutiya wars 1518-1523; annexation; Sadiya Khowa Gohain

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

disputes: Year 1523 vs 1524.
Gait (p. 84 fn.) notes other accounts date the first Chutia invasion to 1516 and name the king Chandra Narayan rather than Dhir Narayan.

events.title: Invasion from Bengal repulsed (Turbak)
events.summary: An army from the Bengal Sultanate under the commander Turbak advanced up the Brahmaputra and was eventually defeated; Turbak was killed. This is the first major clash with a Muslim power from Bengal in Ahom accounts.

sourceRefs.locator: Turbak's invasion from April 1532; death near the Bharali

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

numericClaims.value: thirty elephants, 1,000 horses, artillery and many foot soldiers

disputes: Battle locations and army sizes are not reliably recorded; do not display numbers.

events.title: Ahoms sack the Kachari capital Dimapur
events.summary: After repeated conflict with the Kachari (Dimasa) kingdom, Ahom forces took Dimapur. The Kachari rulers later re-established their capital further south at Maibang. This was a military defeat of the Kacharis, not the annexation of their whole kingdom.

sourceRefs.locator: 1536: Detsung quarrels with the Ahoms; Dimapur sacked
Kachari power broken; Dimapur twice occupied; Marangi Khowa Gohain

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

territorialEffect.notes: Ahom gains in the Dhansiri area; the Kachari kingdom continues independently.

events.summary: Suklenmung moved the royal capital to Garhgaon, which remained the principal capital through the 17th century.

events.title: Koch invasion and temporary occupation of Garhgaon

date.calendarNote: Main invasion January 1563; withdrawal in the autumn (Gait p. 98).

events.summary: In 1562 a Koch fleet under the general Tipu came up the Brahmaputra. In January 1563 Silarai (Chilarai) himself routed the Ahoms; the king fled to Charaikharang in Namrup and Silarai camped in Garhgaon. Three months later peace was made on Koch terms: acknowledgment of Koch supremacy, cession of a large tract on the north bank, hostages from noble families, and an indemnity. Silarai withdrew in the autumn, leaving a garrison at Narayanpur to hold the north-bank cession. The capital was occupied, then given back; the north-bank loss was real.

sourceRefs.locator: Koch invasions 1562-63; Silarai at Garhgaon; terms of peace

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

territorialEffect.notes: Temporary occupation of Garhgaon; formal acknowledgment of Koch supremacy; north-bank tract ceded and garrisoned at Narayanpur.

events.title: Mughals absorb Koch Hajo and reach the Ahom frontier
events.summary: Mughal forces from Bengal defeated Parikshitnarayan of Koch Hajo, bringing the empire's frontier to the Barnadi area and into direct contact with the Ahom kingdom.

sourceRefs.locator: Parikshit's dominions 'as far as the Bar Nadi' annexed; Mughal garrison; Hajo
sourceRefs.note: Year 1612-13 not checked on these pages.

events.title: Ahom-Mughal frontier wars
events.summary: A series of campaigns followed on the western frontier, including Mughal expeditions up the Brahmaputra and Ahom counter-attacks, with fortunes changing several times. Individual engagements, routes and army sizes need case-by-case verification before they are animated.

sourceRefs.locator: chapter 'The Period of the Muhammadan Wars' from Bali Narayan's flight (1615) to the treaty fixing the Bar Nadi boundary

confidence.basis: Overall phase is well documented; individual battles need separate records.

events.title: Paik system reorganised (Pratap Singha and Momai Tamuli Borbarua)
events.summary: During Pratap Singha's reign the paik system of compulsory service was reorganised into a more formal structure of units, an institutional backbone of the 17th-century state.

sourceRefs.locator: Momai-tamuli Barbarua under Pratap Singha; officer grades on the lines of the Mughal mansabdari system
paiks organised in gots of four, reduced to three in Upper Assam under Rajesvar Singh

disputes: Attribution of specific reforms to individuals varies between accounts.

events.title: Peace of 1639: the Barnadi and Asurar Ali boundary
events.summary: A settlement between Momai Tamuli Borbarua and the Mughal commander Allah Yar Khan fixed a boundary: the Barnadi river on the north bank and the Asurar Ali embankment on the south bank, with Guwahati on the Mughal side.

sourceRefs.locator: treaty fixing the Bar Nadi and Asurar Ali as the boundary

events.title: Ahoms occupy Guwahati during the Mughal succession war
events.summary: When Shah Jahan fell ill in 1658 and his sons fought for the throne, Jayadhwaj Singha bridged the Kallang and advanced on Gauhati; the Mughal faujdar fled. Rejecting a Koch offer to share the spoils, the Ahoms drove the Koches back across the Sankosh and, in Gait's words, became masters of the whole Brahmaputra valley for nearly three years.

sourceRefs.locator: Shah Jahan's illness; Jayadhvaj crosses the Kallang; Gauhati taken; Koches driven across the Sankosh

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

events.summary: Mir Jumla, the Mughal governor of Bengal, first occupied Koch Bihar and then, on 4 January 1662, set out for Assam with an army and river fleet. He retook Gauhati and pressed east into the Ahom heartland.

sourceRefs.locator: Mir Jumlah occupies Koch Bihar, then sets out for Assam on 4 January 1662

sourceRefs.note: Edition not yet located - cannot be the sole support.

events.title: Mughal occupation of Garhgaon
events.summary: The Mughal army entered the Ahom capital Garhgaon. Jayadhwaj Singha withdrew to the hills near Namrup. The capital was occupied, but the kingdom was not annexed.

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

events.title: Monsoon, isolation and disease
events.summary: During the monsoon of 1662 the Mughal garrisons in upper Assam were cut off by floods and Ahom raids, and suffered heavily from disease and food shortage.

events.title: Treaty of Ghilajharighat

date.calendarNote: Concluded before 9 January 1663, when Mir Jumla ordered the return (Gait p. 137). 23 January is given in some later works, which conflicts with this.

The terms were only partly carried out.

events.title: Mughal withdrawal and Mir Jumla's death
events.summary: On 9 January 1663 Mir Jumla ordered the army back to Bengal. He fell ill on the way and died on 30 March 1663, just before his ship reached Dacca. Jayadhwaj Singha returned to his capital. The occupation of the Ahom heartland was over.

sourceRefs.locator: return ordered 9 January 1663; Mir Jumlah dies 30 March 1663 just before reaching Dacca

confidence.basis: Standard scholarly account derived from Buranji chronology; page locator not yet verified.

events.title: Guwahati recaptured; Lachit Borphukan in command

date.calendarNote: Bhuyan converts Bhadra 3 and Kartik 17, 1589 Saka as 'near about' 20 Aug and 2 Nov 1667 (pp. 26-27). Approximate to a day or two.

events.summary: In August 1667 Chakradhwaj Singha sent an army west under Lachit, son of the Bar Barua, newly appointed Bar Phukan. Gauhati and Pandu fell after a two-month siege; Mughal reinforcements that arrived in November were defeated and pursued to the Manas. Bhuyan dates the departure to about 20 August and the fall of Itakhuli (Sukreswar Hill) and Gauhati to about 2 November 1667; a stone pillar at Gauhati and a cannon found at Silghat carry inscriptions of Saka 1589 (1667) recording the victory.

sourceRefs.locator: army leaves Bhadra 3, 1589 Saka (c. 20 Aug 1667); Itakhuli and Gauhati fall Kartik 17, 1589 Saka (c. 2 Nov 1667); inscriptions of Saka 1589

confidence.basis: Gait pp. 146-147 and Bhuyan pp. 25-29 agree; Saka 1589 inscriptions are cited by Bhuyan but not yet independently examined (would raise to A).

events.title: Battle of Alaboi

date.calendarNote: Bhuyan's narrative places Alaboi before Chakradhwaj Singha's death in April 1670 (p. 74); his note on a chronicle (Appendix IV) gives c. 29 September 1670 for its first phase. Unresolved.

alternatives.note: Appendix IV chronicle note; conflicts with the narrative order.

events.summary: The Mughal army camped near Alaboi Hill, by Dalibari, on an open plain between the Brahmaputra and the Sesa river. Under pressure from king Chakradhwaj Singha, who doubted his generals' resolve, Lachit sent a large force against it. In the open field, where Mughal and Rajput cavalry had the advantage, the Ahoms suffered a heavy defeat. The Mughals still could not take Gauhati.

events.title: Battle of Saraighat

date.calendarNote: Battle in early 1671; Bhuyan dates Ram Singh's retreat to 23 Chaitra 1592 Saka, 'near about April 5, 1671' (p. 86). Gait: retreat in March 1671 (p. 150).

events.summary: With the Ahom defences around Gauhati breached at Andharubali and Lachit Borphukan gravely ill, the Mughal fleet advanced and Ahom crews began to flee. According to the chronicles followed by Bhuyan, Lachit had himself carried to his boat and led a counter-attack with a handful of war-boats; the rest of the fleet rallied, and the battle was fought on the river between Kamakhya, Itakhuli and Aswakranta. The Mughal fleet was defeated and chased down to Pandu. Ram Singh began his retreat about 5 April 1671. Bhuyan notes that 'Saraighat' was a name loosely used for Gauhati and its surroundings; strictly, Sarai was the village of Amingaon opposite Pandu.

sourceRefs.locator: 'Assamese victory at Saraighat', citing the Assam Buranji (S.M.) pp. 121-124, Kamrupar Buranji, Purani Assam Buranji pp. 147-150, and manuscript Buranjis

events.title: Guwahati handed back to the Mughals
events.summary: During a period of court instability, the Bar Phukan at Gauhati (Laluksola) entered into secret correspondence with the Nawab of Bengal and surrendered Gauhati to the Mughals early in March 1679. Gait notes this is the Ahom version; the Mughal Maasir-i-Alamgiri mentions the 'conquest' without details.

events.title: Battle of Itakhuli

date.calendarNote: Year from cannon inscriptions dated 1604 Saka (Gait p. 161). August is given in later works (unverified here).

alternatives.note: Month from secondary works; verify in Barpujari vol. 2.

events.summary: Gadadhar Singha's army took the Mughal forts near Gauhati and won a great naval victory near the mouth of the Barnadi, capturing the Mughal fleet. The faujdar fled and was pursued to the Manas. Gait calls this the last Muhammadan war: from then on both sides accepted the Manas as the boundary. Two surviving cannon are inscribed as taken by Gadadhar Singha at Gauhati in 1604 Saka (1682).

events.title: Reign of Rudra Singha
events.summary: Rudra Singha's reign is often treated as the height of Ahom power. He developed the capital at Rangpur, sponsored building works and courtly culture, and pursued diplomacy with neighbouring states.

events.title: Kachari and Jaintia campaigns: announced annexation, rising and retreat
events.summary: When the Kachari king Tamradhwaj asserted his independence, Rudra Singha sent two armies, from December 1706, up the Dhansiri and Kopili valleys to the Kachari capital at Maibang; sickness forced a withdrawal. After the Jaintia king seized Tamradhwaj, a second campaign took both kings captive and occupied Jaintiapur, and in February 1708 the Ahoms announced that both kingdoms were annexed. A Jaintia and Khasi rising followed; before the rains the Ahom commanders retreated, destroying Jaintiapur and killing many inhabitants. The annexation did not last.

events.title: Royal religion and satra politics
events.summary: Royal policy towards the Vaishnava monasteries (satras) varied by reign. Gait describes Gadadhar Singha's hostility to the Vaishnava Gosains, and Siva Singha making his queen Phulesvari 'Bar Raja', with coins struck in both names, and her Sakta partisanship. This background mattered for the later Moamoria rebellion.

events.title: Moamoria rebellion: first uprising
events.summary: Followers of the Moamara satra, joined by other discontented groups, rose against the government. In October 1769 Ragha, a Moran leader styling himself Bar Barua, advanced down the north bank; king Lakshmi Singha fled Rangpur but was captured at Sonarinagar. The rebels enthroned Ramakant, who minted coins dated 1691 Saka (1769). In April 1770, on the eve of Bihu, royalists killed Ragha and restored the king, followed by harsh reprisals.

sourceRefs.locator: Ragha's advance, October 1769; king captured at Sonarinagar; Ramakant enthroned; counter-coup April 1770

disputes: Relative weight of religious vs socio-economic causes is debated (Guha vs earlier accounts).

events.title: Second uprising; king flees to Guwahati
events.summary: After an abortive rising in April 1782, a far more serious Moamoria revolt broke out early in 1786. The rebels reached the gates of Rangpur and Gaurinath Singha fled in panic to Gauhati, while the Burha Gohain Purnananda held out on the Namdang until March 1788. The rebel king Bharat Singh later minted coins dated 1793, which survive.

sourceRefs.locator: abortive rising April 1782; serious revolt early 1786; Gaurinath flees to Gauhati; Namdang line held until March 1788

confidence.basis: Gait pp. 190-195 verified.

events.title: Captain Welsh's expedition
events.summary: At Gaurinath Singha's request the East India Company sent Captain Thomas Welsh with sepoys in September 1792. He reached Goalpara on 8 November and took Gauhati in December 1792, and restored the king at Rangpur in March 1794. Under the new Governor-General, Sir John Shore, the Company reversed policy and recalled him; the expedition was back in British territory on 3 July 1794. It was a limited intervention, not a takeover.

events.title: End of the rebellion and the Matak settlement
events.summary: Under the minister Purnananda Burhagohain the government fought on: a 1799 outbreak at Bengmara was defeated, and in 1805 a combined Moamaria and Kachari force was beaten. In the same year Moran Moamarias east of the Dibru rose under Sarbananda Singh at Bengmara; in the end Purnananda gave him the title Bar Senapati, and he collected and paid revenue from the people under him. This became the semi-autonomous Matak territory. The kingdom emerged badly weakened.

events.title: Third Burmese invasion and occupation
events.summary: Fearing for his safety, Chandrakanta fled in April 1821, and the Burmese set up Jogeswar Singha in his place. Chandrakanta fought back and reoccupied Gauhati in January 1822, but in spring 1822 Mingi Maha Bandula arrived from Ava with reinforcements and defeated him at Mahgarh in June. Burmese occupation of the valley followed.
